nodes.label: The Ikhshidids collapse
nodes.full: Egypt's Ikhshidid state, broken by famine and a succession failure, offers no serious resistance when a Fatimid army finally marches from Ifriqiya in 969.
nodes.src: background; Brett, "The Rise of the Fatimids" (2001)

nodes.label: The Almoravids rise in Morocco
nodes.full: A Saharan reform movement builds a new Moroccan empire from the 1050s on, and over the following decades diverts the trans-Saharan gold trade away from the routes feeding Fatimid Ifriqiya and Egypt.
nodes.src: background; Messier, "The Almoravids and the Meanings of Jihad" (2010)

nodes.label: Al-Mahdi founds the dynasty in Ifriqiya
nodes.full: The Ismaili missionary movement, organised for decades in secret, brought its hidden imam out of hiding in 909: backed by the Kutama Berbers, Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i overthrew the Aghlabids and installed Abd Allah as al-Mahdi, caliph and imam.

nodes.label: Al-Qa'im, al-Mansur and the revolt of Abu Yazid
nodes.full: A Kharijite Berber rising under Abu Yazid, 'the man on the donkey', overran Ifriqiya and besieged the Fatimids in Mahdia for months in 944-45. Al-Mansur broke the revolt, founded al-Mansuriyya, and stabilised the state for the conquest of Egypt.

nodes.label: Al-Mu'izz conquers Egypt and builds Cairo
nodes.full: Al-Mu'izz's general Jawhar took Egypt from the failing Ikhshidids in 969, laid out the walled palace-city al-Qahira, and founded al-Azhar. The caliph followed in 973, and the Fatimid centre of gravity moved east for good.

nodes.label: Al-Aziz — the empire at its widest
nodes.full: Under al-Aziz the Fatimid name was read in the Friday prayer from Ifriqiya to Damascus, Mecca and Medina. He staffed the state with Christians and Jews — his vizier Ya'qub ibn Killis was a convert from Judaism — and married a Christian whose brothers he made patriarchs.

nodes.label: Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
nodes.full: Al-Hakim ruled by sudden, contradictory decree: persecutions of Sunnis, then Christians and Jews (the Holy Sepulchre destroyed in 1009), then reversals; bans on chess and on women leaving their houses. In 1021 he rode into the Muqattam hills and never returned.

nodes.label: Al-Zahir, Sitt al-Mulk and the drift
nodes.full: Al-Hakim's sister Sitt al-Mulk governed as regent for the boy al-Zahir and steadied the state after the previous reign's chaos. Her death in 1023 left the government to a rotating set of officials and the beginnings of a long weakening.

nodes.label: Al-Mustansir — the 58-year reign and the collapse
nodes.full: The longest reign in Islamic history spanned the dynasty's ruin and rescue: seven years of Nile failure and famine in the 1060s, the army's regiments fighting each other through a starving Cairo, the loss of Ifriqiya and Syria — until Badr al-Jamali seized the state in 1074.

nodes.label: The Nizari-Musta'li split and al-Musta'li
nodes.full: When al-Mustansir died, the vizier al-Afdal set aside the designated heir Nizar and enthroned his younger brother al-Musta'li. Nizar revolted from Alexandria, was defeated and walled up alive. The Ismaili world split permanently.

nodes.label: Al-Amir to al-Adid — the caliphate as a token
nodes.full: The last five caliphs were installed as children and kept as sacred figureheads while viziers fought for the palace. Al-Amir was murdered by Nizari agents in 1130, splitting the Musta'li da'wa again. By the 1160s the caliph was a prize contested between Jerusalem and Zangid Syria.

nodes.label: Ya'qub ibn Killis builds the Fatimid state
nodes.full: A convert to Islam from a Baghdadi Jewish family, Ibn Killis organised Fatimid Egypt's finances, its land tax, its chancery and its court ceremonial, and turned al-Azhar into a teaching institution with salaried scholars.

nodes.label: Badr al-Jamali — the vizier of the sword
nodes.full: Summoned from Acre with his Armenian troops, Badr al-Jamali crushed the mutinous regiments, ended the famine-era anarchy, rebuilt Cairo's stone walls, and made the vizierate a military dictatorship. The caliph kept the sanctity; the vizier kept the power.

nodes.label: Al-Afdal Shahanshah
nodes.full: Badr's son ruled Egypt for twenty-seven years. He engineered the 1094 succession that split the Ismailis, retook Jerusalem from the Seljuks in 1098 — a year before the Crusaders took it from him — and was assassinated in a Cairo street in 1121.

nodes.label: The vizier-warlords
nodes.full: After al-Afdal the vizierate was seized by force again and again — al-Ma'mun al-Bata'ihi, Ridwan, Ibn Sallar, the regicide Abbas, and Tala'i ibn Ruzzik. Each ruled as regent for a boy caliph; most died violently.

nodes.label: Shawar, Dirgham and the invitation of foreign armies
nodes.full: The last vizier war — Shawar against Dirgham — dragged in both Amalric of Jerusalem and Nur al-Din of Aleppo. Zangid and Crusader armies marched up and down Egypt; Fustat was burned by its own governor (1168); the Zangid general Shirkuh emerged as vizier.

nodes.label: Saladin ends the caliphate
nodes.full: Shirkuh died within months; his nephew Saladin became vizier for the fourteen-year-old al-Adid. In September 1171 Saladin had the Friday sermon read in the name of the Abbasid caliph; al-Adid died days later. The Ismaili caliphate was over.

nodes.label: The revolt of Abu Yazid
nodes.full: A Zanata Berber schoolmaster preaching a rigorist Kharijite Islam raised the tribes of the Aurès against the Fatimids, took Kairouan, and besieged the caliph al-Qa'im in Mahdia. Al-Mansur's counter-offensive, and Abu Yazid's death in 947, saved a dynasty that had come within a wall of ending.

nodes.label: Jawhar takes Egypt
nodes.full: With the Ikhshidid state broken, the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli marched from Ifriqiya, negotiated the surrender of Fustat, and began laying out the palace-city and al-Azhar the same year — the least costly conquest of a great province in the medieval Islamic world.

nodes.label: The Qarmatians invade Egypt
nodes.full: The Qarmatians of eastern Arabia, though fellow Ismailis, rejected the Fatimid claim to the imamate and twice invaded Egypt, reaching the walls of the new capital. Jawhar's defence in 971 and al-Mu'izz's victory in 974 secured the Fatimid hold.

nodes.label: The long contest for Aleppo and Damascus
nodes.full: Fatimid Syria was never secure: the Hamdanids of Aleppo, Bedouin confederations, Byzantine emperors and the Fatimids' own troops all fought over it for decades. The northern frontier drained the treasury without ever being fixed.

nodes.label: The destruction of the Holy Sepulchre
nodes.full: Al-Hakim ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre razed to the rock. Later restored with Byzantine money, the act nonetheless entered Latin memory as an outrage and is counted among the long-fuse causes of the First Crusade eighty years later.

nodes.label: The army's civil wars and the starving of Cairo
nodes.full: Seven years of low Nile met a fractured army — Turkish, Berber and Black African regiments that had stopped obeying anyone. They fought each other through the capital and blockaded the food supply. The Fatimid state effectively dissolved until Badr al-Jamali reconstituted it by force.

nodes.label: The Seljuks take Fatimid Syria and Palestine
nodes.full: As the Fatimid state collapsed inward, the Seljuk Turks took Damascus (1076), Jerusalem and most of Palestine. Al-Afdal recovered Jerusalem and Ascalon from them only in 1098 — just in time to lose Jerusalem to the Crusaders the following year.

nodes.label: The Crusaders take Jerusalem; the Battle of Ascalon
nodes.full: The First Crusade stormed Fatimid Jerusalem in July 1099 and massacred its population. Al-Afdal's relief army arrived weeks late and was routed outside Ascalon. The Fatimids had misjudged the Franks as a possible counterweight to the Seljuks.

nodes.label: The fifty-year war for the coast
nodes.full: The Fatimids held the coastal cities one by one until they could not: Acre fell in 1104, Sidon in 1110, Tyre in 1124, and finally Ascalon — the forward base resupplied by fleet four times a year — in 1153. The navy fought on but the strategic initiative was gone.

nodes.label: The Zangid-Crusader contest for Egypt
nodes.full: Three times between 1164 and 1169 the Zangid general Shirkuh and King Amalric of Jerusalem marched armies into Egypt, each invited by one Fatimid faction against the other. The last campaign ended with Fustat burned, Amalric bought off, and Shirkuh — then Saladin — installed as vizier.

nodes.label: Al-Nu'man codifies Ismaili law
nodes.full: The chief judge al-Qadi al-Nu'man compiled the 'Pillars of Islam' (Da'a'im al-Islam), the official law code of the Fatimid state — a full Shia jurisprudence with the living imam as its ultimate authority.

nodes.label: The da'wa — a hierarchy of missionaries
nodes.full: The Fatimid state ran a graded missionary organisation — a chief da'i in Cairo directing regional da'is who directed local ones. It reached from the Maghreb to Sind, working openly where the Fatimids ruled and in deep secret in Abbasid lands.

nodes.label: The gold dinar as international money
nodes.full: The Fatimid dinar, struck from West African gold and held to a strict standard, became the most trusted coin in the medieval Mediterranean — the 'bezant' Italian and Byzantine merchants preferred and Crusader states later imitated.

nodes.label: Badr al-Jamali and the iqta
nodes.full: To pay an army the bankrupt treasury could not fund in cash, Badr al-Jamali assigned officers the tax revenue of districts directly and had Egypt re-surveyed. It militarised the countryside and set the fiscal pattern the Ayyubids and Mamluks would inherit.

nodes.label: The dhimma under the Fatimids — and under al-Hakim
nodes.full: For most of the dynasty, Christians and Jews served at the highest levels — as viziers, physicians, financiers — and their communities flourished. Al-Hakim's decade of persecution was a violent exception his own successors reversed.
nodes.src: the Geniza; Yahya of Antioch; Rustow (2020)

nodes.label: The imam as the living interpreter
nodes.full: Ismaili doctrine held that scripture and law are the outer shell of a hidden truth that only the imam of the age — present, infallible, descended from Ali and Fatima — can unlock. The Fatimid caliph was, to his followers, the axis on which the cosmos turned.

nodes.label: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man and the founding texts
nodes.full: Al-Nu'man served four caliphs as judge and propagandist and wrote the corpus the Fatimid religious state stood on: the law code, its allegorical interpretation, the history of the da'wa, and the record of the imams' teaching sessions.

nodes.label: The philosopher-missionaries
nodes.full: Ismaili thinkers wove Neoplatonism into the doctrine of the imamate: al-Sijistani's cosmology of the Word, and al-Kirmani's 'Repose of the Intellect' (c.1020), which mapped ten cosmic intellects onto the ten highest ranks of the da'wa.

nodes.label: The Druze — the movement around al-Hakim
nodes.full: A group of da'is — Hamza ibn Ali and al-Darazi — began preaching around 1017 that al-Hakim was the incarnation of the divine. Suppressed in Egypt, the movement 'closed its door' in 1043 and survived in the mountains of Syria and Lebanon.

nodes.label: The da'wa splits — Nizari, Hafizi, Tayyibi
nodes.full: Two succession disputes fractured the movement: 1094 sent the Persian and Syrian da'wa off after Nizar (the future Assassins), and 1130 split the remaining Musta'lis into a Hafizi branch loyal to Cairo and a Tayyibi branch led from Yemen.

nodes.label: The Sunni majority the Fatimids did not convert
nodes.full: Al-Azhar taught Ismaili law, but most Egyptians stayed Sunni, and the Fatimid state made little effort to change that. Two centuries of Ismaili rule left Egypt's population Sunni, which is why Saladin's restoration met almost no resistance.

nodes.label: The Coptic church under Fatimid rule
nodes.full: The Coptic Orthodox church kept its patriarch, its monasteries and its scribes, and supplied the Fatimid administration with clerks and financiers. Al-Hakim's persecution aside, the Fatimid centuries were a period of Coptic cultural consolidation.
nodes.src: "History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria"; Swanson (2010)

nodes.label: The Jewish communities and the Palestinian and Babylonian rites
nodes.full: Fatimid Egypt was the centre of Mediterranean Jewish life. The head of the Jews was recognised by the caliph; both rabbinic rites operated; and the Ben Ezra synagogue's storeroom preserved the papers of that world — the Cairo Geniza.

nodes.label: Cairo — the walled palace-city
nodes.full: Cairo began as a rectangle of mud-brick wall enclosing two vast palaces and the elite regiments — closed to the ordinary population of Fustat next door. Badr al-Jamali rebuilt the walls and three monumental gates in dressed stone in 1087.

nodes.label: Al-Azhar and the Fatimid mosque
nodes.full: Al-Azhar was the congregational mosque of the new capital and a school of the da'wa; the al-Hakim mosque gave the city a second sanctuary; and the small al-Aqmar mosque of 1125 has the first fully composed decorative street facade in Cairo.

nodes.label: Fatimid rock crystal
nodes.full: Fatimid lapidaries carved ewers, bottles and lamps from single flawless blocks of quartz, worked so thin the light passed through. When the palace treasuries were looted in the 1060s crisis, these objects scattered across the Mediterranean.

nodes.label: Lustre pottery, carved wood and tiraz
nodes.full: Fustat's workshops produced lustre-painted bowls, carved wooden panels with painted hunting scenes, and inscribed tiraz textiles issued as robes of honour. Fatimid ornament spread to Norman Sicily and beyond.

nodes.label: The Fatimid ceremonial calendar
nodes.full: The Fatimid state governed by procession: the caliph rode out for the two Eids, the opening of the Nile canal, the Nilometer readings, Ashura and the mawlid. The city's year was a liturgy performed by the imam.

nodes.label: The poets of the da'wa and the court
nodes.full: Ibn Hani al-Andalusi praised al-Mu'izz in verse that verged on deifying him; the traveller-poet Nasir Khusraw became a da'i; and the vizier Tala'i ibn Ruzzik was a respected poet. Ismaili doctrine gave Fatimid panegyric a cosmic register.

nodes.label: Ibn al-Haytham and the Book of Optics
nodes.full: Ibn al-Haytham came to Cairo under al-Hakim. There he wrote the 'Book of Optics', which established by systematic experiment that vision works by light entering the eye, and described the camera obscura — a founding document of the experimental method.

nodes.label: Ibn Yunus and the Hakimi tables
nodes.full: The astronomer Ibn Yunus compiled the 'Hakimi Zij', the most careful set of astronomical tables of its age, based on decades of his own recorded observations — used a thousand years later to measure the slowing of the Earth's rotation.

nodes.label: The House of Knowledge
nodes.full: Al-Hakim founded the Dar al-Ilm, a public library and teaching institution stocked from the palace collections and open to scholars of every discipline and, it seems, every faith.

nodes.label: The Cairo-Baghdad medical dispute
nodes.full: Ali ibn Ridwan, a self-taught Cairo physician, carried on a famous long-distance quarrel with the Baghdad doctor Ibn Butlan over Galen and the value of book-learning versus apprenticeship.

nodes.label: The Brethren of Purity enter the Ismaili canon
nodes.full: The 'Epistles of the Brethren of Purity', the Basran encyclopedia of the sciences, were taken up by the Fatimid and especially the later Tayyibi da'wa as an authoritative statement of the cosmos the imam presides over.

nodes.label: The chroniclers of Fatimid Egypt — mostly writing later
nodes.full: The great contemporary chronicle, al-Musabbihi's 13,000-page history, survives only in a single volume and in quotation. The connected narrative comes from Ibn Muyassar and al-Maqrizi, five centuries removed.

nodes.label: The India trade moves to the Red Sea
nodes.full: Under the Fatimids the long-distance trade with India and the Far East shifted decisively from the Persian Gulf to the Red Sea route through Aden, up to the Egyptian ports and across to Alexandria. Cairo-Fustat became the great clearing-house.

nodes.label: The Cairo Geniza — a documented commercial world
nodes.full: For religious reasons the Jews of Fustat did not throw away paper bearing the name of God — and so kept, in a synagogue storeroom, tens of thousands of ordinary documents. It is the fullest picture of everyday medieval Mediterranean life that exists.

nodes.label: West African gold
nodes.full: The gold that backed the Fatimid dinar came across the Sahara from the Sahel through the caravan city of Sijilmasa. Control of that flow was a Fatimid war aim in the Maghreb, and its later diversion toward Almoravid Morocco was one cause of Ifriqiya's decline.

nodes.label: The Mustansirite famine
nodes.full: Seven successive low Niles, compounded by the army's blockade of the food supply and by plague, produced the worst famine in Egypt's recorded medieval history. The state did not function for a decade.

nodes.label: Fustat — a manufacturing and warehousing city
nodes.full: Below the royal enclosure of al-Qahira, Fustat was where the work was done: apartment blocks, glass and pottery kilns, sugar refineries, paper mills, and the warehouses where India and Mediterranean goods were stored and taxed.

nodes.label: The Italian merchants in Alexandria
nodes.full: Amalfitans first, then Venetians, Pisans and Genoese, kept warehouses and consuls in Alexandria and carried Egyptian alum, flax, sugar and spices to Europe against silver and timber.

nodes.label: The experimental method in optics
nodes.full: Ibn al-Haytham's optics is not just a theory but a method: darkened rooms, apertures, tubes, screens and sighting instruments used to test claims against controlled observation. It is the clearest medieval statement anywhere of science as deliberate experiment.

nodes.label: A city built on paper
nodes.full: Fatimid Egypt ran on cheap paper: the chancery's decrees, the merchants' letters, the shopping lists later found in the Geniza. Egyptian paper mills supplied the eastern Mediterranean.

nodes.label: The Fatimid war fleet
nodes.full: The Fatimids maintained a standing Mediterranean navy — a state arsenal, salaried crews, and squadrons that fought the Byzantines, raided the crusader coast and resupplied Ascalon four times a year until it fell.

nodes.label: The stone walls and gates of Cairo
nodes.full: Badr al-Jamali's rebuilding of Cairo's enceinte in cut stone, with rounded and rectangular towers, brought Byzantine-frontier military architecture — carried by his Armenian engineers — into Egypt.

nodes.label: The da'wa as a trans-regional network
nodes.full: The Fatimid missionary organisation was the connective tissue of a movement no single state could contain: da'is in Yemen, Sind, Bahrain, Khurasan and the Maghreb, reporting toward Cairo. Nasir Khusraw was recruited into it in Cairo and sent home to run the da'wa of Khurasan.

nodes.label: The Armenians come to Egypt
nodes.full: Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian, brought Armenian regiments, officials and their families to Egypt, and his son al-Afdal continued the settlement. Armenian viziers, an Armenian Coptic-rite church and Armenian craftsmen took root in Fatimid Cairo.

nodes.label: The Sulayhid queen of Yemen
nodes.full: Arwa bint Ahmad, al-Sayyida al-Hurra, ruled Yemen for some seventy years as a Fatimid vassal, held the da'wa rank of hujja, and minted coins. When the Musta'li da'wa split in 1132, the Tayyibi branch entrusted its leadership to her.

nodes.label: Byzantium — the peace across the frontier
nodes.full: After the frontier fighting of the 960s-980s the Fatimids and Byzantines settled into a long working peace: trade treaties, an agreed protectorate over Aleppo, Byzantine grain in famine years, and — after al-Hakim — Byzantine money rebuilding the Holy Sepulchre.

nodes.label: The Fatimids and the Franks
nodes.full: The Fatimids first approached the passing Crusaders as possible allies against the Seljuks, then fought them for sixty years over the coast, then took a Frankish garrison into Cairo and paid Jerusalem tribute against the Zangid threat.

nodes.label: Fatimid style travels — Sicily and beyond
nodes.full: Fatimid ornament, ceramics, textiles and the muqarnas vault reached Norman Sicily directly — the painted ceiling of the Cappella Palatina in Palermo is Fatimid work or close imitation — and Fatimid rock crystal entered European treasuries.

nodes.label: Three caliphates at once
nodes.full: The Fatimid proclamation of 909 broke the fiction of a single caliph; the Umayyad ruler of Córdoba answered with his own claim in 929. For the rest of the Middle Ages there were at least two, often three, men each insisting he alone led all Muslims.

nodes.label: The centre of gravity moves to Cairo
nodes.full: The founding of Cairo created the city that would be the largest and richest in the Islamic world for six centuries — the seat of the Fatimid, then Ayyubid, then Mamluk states, and the hinge of the India trade.

nodes.label: The Seljuk squeeze
nodes.full: The arrival of the Sunni Seljuks in Syria caught the Fatimids between a resurgent Abbasid orthodoxy and their own internal collapse. They lost Damascus, Jerusalem and the interior of Palestine, recovering only the coast.

nodes.label: The Crusades and the Fatimid misjudgement
nodes.full: Cairo read the First Crusade as another band of Frankish mercenaries who might be turned against the Seljuks, and opened negotiations. By the time the mistake was clear the Crusaders held Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Egypt returns to Sunni Islam
nodes.full: Saladin's suppression of the caliphate in 1171 met almost no resistance because the Ismaili state had never made Egypt Ismaili. Within a generation the Ayyubids had covered Cairo in Sunni madrasas and the Fatimid palaces had become barracks.

nodes.label: The afterlives of the Fatimid da'wa
nodes.full: The state ended in 1171 but the movement did not: the Nizari line produced the Aga Khans; the Tayyibi line, carried to Gujarat, produced the Bohra communities; and the Druze survived in Syria and Lebanon.

nodes.label: Women of power — Sitt al-Mulk and Queen Arwa
nodes.full: Al-Hakim's sister Sitt al-Mulk ran the Egyptian state as regent after his disappearance; the Sulayhid queen Arwa ruled Yemen for seventy years and held the da'wa rank of hujja, the highest a person other than the imam could reach.

nodes.label: The Geniza people
nodes.full: The Geniza lets us follow individuals: the India trader Abraham Ben Yiju, a widow petitioning the court over her dowry, a schoolboy's copybook. It is medieval life at eye level, in the words of the people living it.

nodes.label: The ethnic regiments and the army that tore the state apart
nodes.full: The Fatimid army was a mosaic of recruited and enslaved groups kept deliberately separate — Kutama Berbers, Turkish and Daylami cavalry, Black African infantry, then Armenians. Under a weak caliph in a famine they fought each other rather than the enemy.

nodes.label: Slavery in the Fatimid world
nodes.full: Enslaved people reached Egypt down the Nile from Nubia, across the Red Sea from the Horn, and by the Mediterranean from Europe: military slaves, eunuch officials, and domestic slaves whose lives fill the Geniza's marriage contracts and manumission deeds.

nodes.label: The palace eunuchs
nodes.full: Eunuchs — enslaved as boys, castrated outside the empire, raised in the palace — held some of the highest offices of the Fatimid state: tutors of caliphs, keepers of the treasuries, commanders of armies.

nodes.label: Al-Hakim — the caliph as an enigma
nodes.full: No medieval Muslim ruler is harder to read than al-Hakim: an ascetic who gave away his wealth; a persecutor who made restitution; a lawgiver whose followers declared him God and who vanished, at 36, into the hills.
